title: The US Just Dropped Fraud Charges Against Gautam Adani. His Stock Surged 22 Per Cent in May. Here Is What NRI Investors Should Understand About What Happened.
excerpt: The DOJ criminal case is closed, the SEC has settled, and the Treasury resolved an Iran sanctions case for $275 million. Bernstein says the worst is over. But the Adani saga reshaped how global capital views Indian conglomerates — and that lesson has not been unlearned.
body:
In November 2024, the United States Department of Justice unsealed a criminal indictment against Gautam Adani, alleging that the billionaire and his co-defendants had defrauded investors by concealing a $265 million bribery scheme tied to solar energy contracts in India. The Securities and Exchange Commission filed a parallel civil case. Adani Group stocks lost billions in market value within hours.

Six months later, all three US legal actions against the Adani Group have been resolved. The DOJ has dropped criminal fraud charges. The SEC has reached a settlement. The US Treasury Department has settled a separate case involving the purchase of sanctioned Iranian energy, with Adani Enterprises agreeing to pay $275 million. Adani Enterprises surged 22 per cent in May, the single largest monthly gainer on the Nifty 50.

For the millions of NRI investors who hold Adani Group stocks directly or through mutual funds and ETFs, the legal cloud that hung over the conglomerate for 18 months has lifted. But the story is more complicated than a simple vindication.

## What Actually Happened in the US Courts

The DOJ's original indictment charged Gautam Adani, his nephew Sagar Adani, and former Adani Green Energy CEO Vneet Jaain with securities fraud and conspiracy. The alleged scheme involved paying bribes to Indian state government officials to secure contracts for a 12-gigawatt solar energy project, then raising billions from US investors without disclosing the corruption.

The case faced jurisdictional challenges from the start. Adani's legal team argued that the alleged bribery occurred entirely in India, that no US investors lost money, and that the defendants had no direct involvement in marketing securities to American buyers. Several of the SEC's claims were challenged as "non-actionable puffery" — corporate statements about ESG commitments and anti-corruption practices that investors could not reasonably rely on.

The DOJ's decision to drop the case aligns with a broader pattern under the current administration, which has deprioritised foreign bribery prosecution. The DOJ also recently dismissed the long-running FIFA bribery case, stating that foreign corruption cases no longer fit the administration's enforcement priorities.

Indian-American business leaders welcomed the outcome. "There was no evidence of bribery. There were assumptions made, and you can't move forward on assumptions unless you have real evidence," said Dr Mukesh Aghi, President of the US-India Strategic Partnership Forum. "No investors, especially US investors, lost any money."

## The Market Impact

Adani Enterprises was the standout performer in what was otherwise a difficult month for Indian equities. The Nifty 50 fell 1.9 per cent in May and the Sensex shed 2.8 per cent — their worst May in three years — as uncertainty over the US-Iran conflict, elevated oil prices, and the MSCI rebalancing weighed on sentiment.

The MSCI Emerging Markets index rejig, which took effect on Friday May 29, cut India's weight from approximately 20 per cent to 11.2 per cent, triggering significant passive outflows. Heavyweight stocks including Reliance Industries (down 7.7 per cent), ONGC (down 11.4 per cent), and ITC (down 8.9 per cent) all posted sharp monthly declines.

Against that backdrop, the Adani Group's rally was an outlier driven by a specific catalyst. Bernstein, the research firm, issued a note stating that "the worst may be over" for the conglomerate, citing the resolution of US legal overhangs and the group's dominant position in infrastructure sectors including ports, power, and renewable energy.

The $275 million Treasury settlement over Iranian energy purchases is the only penalty the group has actually paid. It is a significant sum, but manageable for a conglomerate with a combined market capitalisation exceeding $200 billion.

## What NRI Investors Should Consider

The legal resolution removes uncertainty, which markets price efficiently. But it does not retroactively validate the Adani Group's governance practices or corporate transparency — the issues that short-seller Hindenburg Research raised in January 2023 and that the US indictment amplified.

For NRI investors holding Adani stocks, there are three key considerations going forward.

First, the reputational risk premium that had been priced into Adani Group stocks since the Hindenburg report will continue to deflate. This is positive for valuations in the near term.

Second, the group's access to international capital markets has improved substantially. With no active US legal proceedings, Adani Green Energy and other group entities can raise dollar-denominated debt more easily and at lower spreads. Adani Group's $70 billion clean energy investment target by 2030 depends on this access.

Third, the broader lesson of the saga — that concentrated exposure to a single Indian conglomerate carries risks that are difficult to model — remains valid. Diversification across the Indian market, rather than concentrated bets on any single group, remains the most prudent approach for NRI portfolios.

## The Bigger Picture

The Adani case was never just about one company. It became a proxy for the India-US economic relationship, for the question of whether US extraterritorial legal reach would deter investment in Indian companies, and for the debate over governance standards in India's largest conglomerates.

The resolution is being framed by both sides as a diplomatic win. Indian business leaders see it as a correction of prosecutorial overreach. US officials have moved on to other priorities. The practical effect is that the largest private infrastructure builder in India can now operate without a legal overhang that was beginning to affect deal flow.

For the Indian diaspora investor community, the takeaway is nuanced. The charges were dropped, but the scrutiny they triggered — into related-party transactions, share pledging, and corporate complexity — has permanently raised the bar for transparency that the market demands from Indian conglomerates. That is not a bad outcome.
author: Diaspora Desk
